## Research Questions

How many feral hogs are there, and where are they located? - We are curious what the extent of the issue is, and where is it most affecting the land and people in the US. This will guide what kinds of damage we look into and motivate other questions.

What is the extent of the potential damage to land and crops?\
- We are interested in how much are feral swine affecting their habitat and what their risks are to crops. We were unable to find much data in crop damage, but do understand that they pose a risk to farmland.

Where might feral hogs migrate to, and what is at risk? - We want to know what changes may be coming to the populations, and how those dynamics may alter future damages. How can data better inform future planning and remediation efforts.

## Ethical Concerns

Neither of us are from the area where feral swine run rampant in the US nor have either of us have make a livelihood off of feral swine or the crops that the damage. We acknowledge that the feral swine found in the United States (Sus Scrofa) are an invasive species brought to the United States by European settlers for game hunting and this introduction has impacted the local ecosystems. Our project is merely a capstone project. We do not have the resource or access to data that would make our predictions truly accurate, thus our results should not be used to make any future decisions regarding the eradication or management of the United States feral swine population.

## Data Cleaning

We have cleaned a few separate sets of data for our purposes in this project. All code for cleaning can be found in the `cleaning` file and cleaned data is in the `data/clean` folder. We have a list of counties that recorded feral swine from 2021-2025, this was attained from the USDA. We also have some climate data by county, that could potentially used to help build out the models for predicting feral swine. Also in that file, there is code for cleaning USDA data about production of wheat, corn and soybean by county, which could be used to analyze risk and evaluate our second question. We also have the shape files of US counties, acquired from the US census bureau.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
head(read_csv("../data/clean/crop_production.csv"))
head(read_csv("../data/clean/climate_county.csv"))
head(read_csv("../data/clean/combined_counties.csv"))
```

The *crop_production* data set has, for each county and year pair, the numbers of bushels of each crop type (wheat, corn, and soybean) produced in that year. This data will help us figure out which crops feral swine seem to be drawn to and help us calculate potential damages. Obtained using the USDA's quickstat website.

The *climate_county* data set contains temperature and precipitation data, which we will use when determining suitability for the feral swine population and in our predictive models. Data obtained from NOAA.

The *combined_counties* data set contains the swine presence for each county in the United states for every year in our time frame. This is the main data set we will be working with throughout the course of our project. This data was acquired from the USDA's National Feral Swine Damage Management Program. This data is not publicly available, but was given to us by request.

In the following we both use the same us county boundaries shape files for our maps and anything regarding spacial information. This was obtained from Data.gov.

## Non-Spatial Model

```{r}

swine_climate <- read_csv("../data/clean/climate_county.csv") |> 
  left_join(read_csv("../data/clean/combined_counties.csv")) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), ~if_else(is.na(.x), F, T))) |> 
  left_join(read_csv("../data/clean/crop_production.csv") |> 
              mutate(across(where(is.character), ~str_to_title(.x))) |> 
              select(state, county, fullID),
            by = join_by(state, county))


mod <- glm(swine_2025 ~ temp2125 + dailymin2125 + dailymax2125 + precip2125, swine_climate,
           family = binomial())

swine_climate <- swine_climate |> 
   mutate(pred = as.numeric(predict.glm(mod)))

swine_climate_sf <- read_sf("../data/raw/cb_2018_us_county_5m/cb_2018_us_county_5m.shp") |> 
  left_join(swine_climate, by = join_by(GEOID == fullID)) |> 
  filter(STATEFP != "15"& STATEFP != "11" & STATEFP != "02" & STATEFP != "72"
         & STATEFP != "78" & STATEFP != "60" & STATEFP != "66" & STATEFP != "69"
         & GEOID != "53055" & GEOID != "25019")
 
ggplot(swine_climate_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pred))

```

This non-spatial model is just built as a logistic regression predicting swine presence in 2025 based on county-level climate data. The code is not quite running at the moment but I am working on it. I need to clear up some of the ID stuff, but it is mostly working.

# Spatial Model

## Background

Using the machine learning algorithms that are taught in STAT 212: Statistical Machine learning, we can develop regression models that can predict future state based off of prior data. However, what the models in STAT 212 lack is a spacial component. What spacial machine learning models help us incorporate spacial relations into the model, having the regression of one space be dependent on both its prior trends and those of its neighbors.

For our project, we will be using a spacial machine learning algorithm because feral swine, without the aide of humans, cannot move from one county to the other without the counties sharing a border of some sort. Since our question focuses on migration, a spacial model will take into consideration where the swine are located currently and evaluate the potential for the neighboring counties to have swine other than each county's individual risk of a feral swine invasion without considering the location.

## Running Spacial Machine Learning Algorithms

## Steps for Running Spacial Machine Learning Algorithms

#### Step 1: Determine Spacial Autocorrelation

We first must determine spacial autocorrelation before we can even begin to run a spacial machine learning algorithm. Spacial autocorrelation determines if there is a spacial trend in out data or if there is a lack of trend. If there is a lack of a trend, we can not move on with running a spacial machine learning algorithm.

##### Moran's I

Moran's I is a method of determining spacial autocorrelation. A Moran's I value of 0 indicate while -1 and 1 indicate high negative and positive correlation respectively.

Moran's I formula: $I=\frac{n\sum_i\sum_jw_{ij}(Y_i-\bar{Y})(Y_j-\bar{Y})}{(\sum_{i\not=j}w_{ij})\sum_i(Y_i-\bar{Y})^2}$

```{r}
# Loading Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(spdep)
library(sf)
library(mapview)
library(sp)
library(rlist)
```

```{r}
# Loading Data
swine <- read_csv("../data/clean/combined_counties.csv")
us_county <- st_read("../data/raw/cb_2018_us_county_5m/cb_2018_us_county_5m.shp")
```



```{r}
# Putting Data into a usable format
# Making a dataset using only the contiguous United States
# Removing all the counties that are not a part of the lower 48 states or that are islands.
us_48 <- us_county |> 
  filter(STATEFP != "15"& STATEFP != "11" & STATEFP != "02" & STATEFP != "72"
         & STATEFP != "78" & STATEFP != "60" & STATEFP != "66" & STATEFP != "69"
         & GEOID != "53055" & GEOID != "25019")

# Making a dataset of all counties in the united states with their swine presence
swine_counties = swine |> 
  select(county_ID, swine_2020, swine_2021, swine_2022, swine_2023, swine_2024, swine_2025) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), ~as.numeric(.x))) |> # Turing trues and falses into 1s and 0s for regression
  right_join(us_48, join_by(county_ID == GEOID)) |> # joining the swine county data to the rest of the United States Counties
  mutate(swine_2020 = replace_na(swine_2020, 0),
         swine_2021 = replace_na(swine_2021, 0),
         swine_2022 = replace_na(swine_2022, 0),
         swine_2023 = replace_na(swine_2023, 0),
         swine_2024 = replace_na(swine_2024, 0),
         swine_2025 = replace_na(swine_2025, 0)) |> 
  st_as_sf(sf_column_name = "geometry") |> #Changing the geomtry into polygons
  as(Class ="Spatial")

# Mapping to see if the polygons work
mapview(swine_counties, zcol = "swine_2020")
```

This map shows us that the spatial polygons are working and contain the variable of interest. For now, we are just looking at 2020 data to get our bearings on how to code for spacial autocorrelation.

```{r}
# Moran's I
nb <- poly2nb(swine_counties, queen = TRUE)

plot(nb,coordinates(swine_counties))

nbw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

gmoran <- moran.test(swine_counties$swine_2020, nbw,alternative = "greater")
gmoran
```

The map above shows which counties are neighbors to each other (neighbors is defined as sharing a border). The lines show neighbor relations and circles represent counties. Here we see that all the counties are connected to each other, proving that our cleaning of the data to not include counties that are islands and that neighbor no other counties has worked.

From the printed results of the *morgan.test*, we can see that our Moran's I value is $0.8464733027$ which indicates a strong positive spatial autocorrelation which tells us that we can move on with building a spacial model. We will want to repeat this test with the swine data from other years to make sure this statement remains true for all the years in our dataset.

After we run spatial autocorrelation for all of the years of swine data, we can make a model using only the swine data, leaving the most recent year (2025) out to use to test our model's accuracy. Additionally, we plan on making a spacial model that includes other factors such as food availability and landscape to see if adding in habitat features makes or model more accurate in its predictions.

## Crop Data

```{r}
crop_sf <- read_sf("../data/raw/cb_2018_us_county_5m/cb_2018_us_county_5m.shp") |> 
    filter(STATEFP != "15"& STATEFP != "11" & STATEFP != "02" & STATEFP != "72"
         & STATEFP != "78" & STATEFP != "60" & STATEFP != "66" & STATEFP != "69"
         & GEOID != "53055" & GEOID != "25019") |> 
  left_join(
    read_csv("../data/clean/crop_production.csv") |> 
      mutate(ID5 = str_c(stateID, countyID)),
    by = join_by(GEOID == ID5)
    )

ggplot(crop_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = corn))
```

We will make our final maps in ArcGIS, but here is an example of the visualization we could make with the given crop data. We want to be able to work this into the risk factor given by the spatial model to hypothesize what the potential issues are.
